comparisonItems.text: Cooking: electric kettles, mixer grinders, toasters, ovens and microwave ovens.
Lighting: lamps in homes, offices, streets, markets and factories.
Transport and lifting: electric trains, buses, cars, scooters, lifts and escalators.
Heating and cooling: fans, room heaters, immersion heaters, geysers, refrigerators and air conditioners.
Entertainment and communication: televisions, radios, mobile phones and equipment that carries internet signals.
Other work: water pumps, cranes and computers used in schools, hospitals and workplaces.

blocks.text: 3.1  Inside a Torch

1. Take a small battery torch approved by your teacher. Locate its lamp and switch. Predict what moving the switch will do. 2. Move the switch to each position and record what the lamp does. If it does not light, record that too; do not assume the switch is the only possible cause. 3. Switch it off. With your teacher, open only its removable cell compartment. Note the number, direction and markings of the cells before removing them. 4. Draw the parts you can identify in your notebook. Do not force open a sealed or rechargeable torch.

A working torch commonly lights in one switch position and stays dark in the other. Inside are a source, a lamp and conducting connections. The switch changes a connection. To explain why that matters, we need to examine the parts and then trace the complete path through them.

3.2  A Simple Electrical Circuit
Cells and their terminals

1. Inspect an undamaged cylindrical 1.5 V cell supplied by your teacher. Find its + and − markings. Compare the two ends without joining them. 2. Sketch the cell and label the marked ends. Describe the raised metal cap and the flatter metal end. Check your labels against the markings. 3. Look at an empty cell holder. Find its spring contacts and polarity marks. Predict how the cell should fit; ask your teacher to check before inserting it.

An **electric cell** is a source of electrical energy supplied by chemical changes inside it. Its two connection points are **terminals**: positive (+) and negative (−). On the familiar cylindrical cell, the raised metal cap is positive and the flat metal end is negative. Other cell shapes differ, so read the markings rather than relying on shape alone.

An **electric cell** is a source of electrical energy supplied by chemical changes inside it. Its two connection points are **terminals**: positive (+) and negative (−). On the familiar cylindrical cell, the raised metal cap is positive and the flat metal end is negative. Other cell shapes differ, so read the markings rather than relying on shape alone.

The number 1.5 V on a familiar cell is its stated voltage. Voltage describes the energy transferred per amount of charge; here it helps us choose a suitable source and lamp. It is not a count of how much charge remains in a used cell. Two cells with the same printed rating can behave differently if one is depleted or makes poor contact.
A voltmeter measures voltage between the two terminals.

Connecting cells together

1. Use an approved two-cell torch with matching cells. With the switch off, record the original arrangement, then confirm that it works. 2. Switch off and swap the positions of the two cells while keeping each cell’s marked direction correct. Test briefly and record the result. 3. For comparison, draw what would happen if one cell were reversed. Your teacher may demonstrate this briefly in a suitable simple holder; do not reverse cells in electronic devices. 4. Restore the correct arrangement. Compare position with direction: are they the same thing?

In a **series** arrangement, the positive terminal of one cell joins the negative terminal of the next. With two matching 1.5 V cells correctly connected, their voltages add to about 3 V. Their metal links may be hidden inside a holder, even when the cells sit side by side. Follow the connections, not the shape of the case. In everyday use, “battery” can mean one cell or several cells connected together.

Follow the internal route: one terminal connects to a support wire, then to the filament, then through the other support to the other terminal. The insulating part at the base prevents a direct metal bridge between the terminals. Current must pass through the filament for it to heat. This is why touching two wires to the same terminal does not substitute for using both terminals.

Incandescent lamps and LEDs

A torch lamp and an LED can both turn electrical energy into light, but they are not interchangeable in every holder. Their connections and supply requirements differ. Read the component rating with your teacher before substituting one for another. A component that does not light on a particular supply may still work on an appropriate supply; failure in one setup is not enough to call it broken.

An **electrical circuit** includes a path through which current can flow. In arrangements 1 and 6, the two lamp terminals connect to opposite cell terminals, making a complete path through the filament. Reversing the two connections does not prevent a correctly rated incandescent lamp from glowing. In 2 and 3, a connection is missing. In 4 and 5, both lamp terminals go to the same cell terminal, so the cell does not drive current through the lamp.

**Electric current** is the flow of electric charge. By convention, its direction in the external circuit is from the cell’s positive terminal, through the components, towards its negative terminal. A complete loop, a working source and suitable components are all needed. The cell transfers energy to the lamp; current is not a substance that gets used up inside the filament.

A lamp stays dark. One group concludes, “The cell is used up.” Another says, “The wire touches the plastic instead of the metal.” What evidence would distinguish these explanations? Plan a sequence that changes one thing at a time. Include a known working lamp, a known working cell and a contact check. Explain why replacing a cell could also improve a loose connection.

A lamp with a broken filament is often called fused. Its internal path is open even when the outside wires look correct. A dark lamp can also mean a depleted cell, loose or dirty contacts, the wrong lamp rating, or insulation trapped at a contact. A test result becomes more useful when you can rule out these alternatives.

blocks.text: Making an LED light

Your teacher supplies a red LED suitable for a 3 V circuit, two matching 1.5 V cells in a series holder, a 330 Ω resistor and insulated leads. The teacher checks the LED ratings first. 1. Keep the cells disconnected while building. Connect the holder’s positive lead to the resistor, the other resistor end to the LED anode, and the cathode to the holder’s negative lead. 2. Ask your teacher to check the connections. Connect briefly, observe the LED, record the result and disconnect. 3. Your teacher may reverse only the LED for a brief comparison if its reverse-voltage rating permits 3 V. Predict, observe and then disconnect. If that rating is unknown, discuss the comparison using the diagram instead. 4. Restore the approved forward connection. If no light appears, check polarity, contacts and component ratings; do not remove the resistor.
Forward connection: the resistor is in the same loop as the LED. Disconnect before changing any component.

An LED normally conducts readily in its forward direction and emits light when enough current flows. Reversing it usually prevents light at this small supply voltage, but excessive reverse voltage can damage it. The **resistor** limits current and protects the LED. It may be on either side of the LED in this single loop. Correct polarity alone does not make a direct connection to a battery safe.

blocks.text: A switch controls the path

1. Collect thick cardboard, two brass split-pin fasteners, a bare metal paper clip and two insulated wires. Your teacher makes the holes and secures the fasteners, covering any sharp ends underneath. 2. Trap one end of the clip under the first fastener so it can pivot. Place the second fastener where the clip can touch it when turned. 3. Attach one wire to each fastener. Check that the clip moves freely and can leave a visible gap. Build without a cell connected.

You have made a movable connection. Before using it, predict which position will allow a complete path. Inspect the metal contact: painted or plastic-coated clips may fail to conduct at their surfaces, even though there is metal underneath.

1. Join the switch, a correctly rated incandescent lamp and one cell in a single loop. Start with the clip away from the second fastener. Observe and record. 2. Touch the clip to the second fastener. Observe briefly, record and open the switch again. Compare your observations with your prediction. 3. Disconnect the cell, move the switch to a different place in the same loop, and reconnect. Does its position change whether opening it interrupts the path? 4. Disconnect after the test. If the lamp does not respond, check the metal contacts before changing your explanation.

A **switch** completes or breaks a conducting path; it is not the source of energy. In the single-loop circuit here, opening the switch anywhere interrupts current everywhere in that loop. Household switches also control paths, but their construction and installation must meet much greater safety demands. Never open or test a mains switch.

3.3  Reading Circuit Diagrams

A photograph shows what equipment looks like. A **circuit diagram** uses symbols to show how it is connected. The drawing need not match the physical positions of the parts. A long straight line can represent a bent wire; what matters is which terminals it joins.

1. Make a loop with one cell and a matching incandescent lamp, leaving two free wire ends as a test gap. Briefly touch those ends together. If the lamp does not glow, fix the tester before continuing. The lamp must remain in the loop. 2. Choose safe, clean, dry objects: a spoon, coin, key, foil, cork, rubber eraser, plastic ruler, wooden block, glass item, paper, cardboard, wax and graphite pencil lead. Let the teacher handle any pins or needles. 3. Place each object across the gap so the two wire ends touch separate points on it, not each other. Test briefly, record the material and whether the lamp glows, then disconnect. 4. Recheck the tester by touching its free ends together between doubtful results. Describe anything that may affect contact: a coating, dirt, moisture or a very small contact area. 5. Use the recording guide to propose a conclusion and its limits. Never test people, sockets, liquids or connected appliances.

Notebook recording guide: keep observations separate from conclusions

A **conductor** allows electric current to flow relatively easily. An **insulator** resists that flow strongly under the conditions considered. Metals such as copper and aluminium are useful conductors. Dry plastic, rubber, glass and ceramic commonly act as insulators. Graphite is a non-metal that conducts: being metallic is not the definition of a conductor.

Never touch plugs or switches with wet hands, use electrical equipment in wet areas, or handle damaged cords and plugs. Tell an adult about damage and keep away. A cell supplies direct current (DC): in a simple working circuit its direction stays the same. Household supply is alternating current (AC), whose direction reverses repeatedly. DC is not limited to small devices; electric vehicles also use large battery packs. Safety depends on the source and conditions, not merely on the labels AC and DC.

Portable power and responsible use

Cylindrical cells power many torches, clocks, remotes and toys. Button cells are used in some watches and hearing aids; rechargeable packs serve phones, laptops and electric vehicles. Their sizes, arrangements and charging requirements differ. Keep loose cells away from metal objects and small children. Never dismantle a cell or put it in a fire. Give used cells to an adult for an approved collection route.

blocks.text: Explore Further
Two days without mains electricity

Plan for a two-day power cut: consider light, water, communication, food storage and transport. Which activities could use stored energy or another method? Discuss preparation with an adult; never test generators.
A small solar-powered fan

With your teacher, connect a small educational solar panel to a matching low-voltage toy motor and soft propeller. Use the manufacturer’s instructions and secure the motor. Keep fingers, hair and clothing away from moving blades. Compare its behaviour in bright light and partial shade without changing the connections. Record light conditions as well as motion.

Investigate cells in use

Both materials matter

List safe household objects made mainly of conducting materials, mainly of insulating materials, or of both. Identify the purpose of each part in the mixed group. Observe externally; do not open plugs or appliances. Explain why “made of both” is often a useful design rather than a contradiction. A plastic handle and a metal working part can serve different purposes; identify each material before deciding what the whole object tells you.
